config.prompt: Explain, in a few paragraphs, how a write-ahead log lets a database recover after a crash.

reference.text:
In a write-ahead log, changes to the database are written to a log file before they are written to the database itself. This ensures that if the database crashes before the changes are written to the database, the log file can be used to recover the data. When the database comes back online, it can read the log file and apply the changes to the database, effectively recovering the lost data.
This approach is called "write-ahead" because the database writes the changes to the log first, ahead of writing them to the database. This ensures that the log always reflects the latest changes, even if the database itself is not up to date. If a crash occurs, the database can start again from the point where it was last consistent, by applying the changes in the log file to the database.
The write-ahead log is typically used in conjunction with a checkpoint mechanism, which periodically writes the changes in the log file to the database, so that the database is up to date. This ensures that the database is always consistent, and can recover from a crash by applying the changes in the log file.

## Step 1: Introduction to Write-Ahead Logging
A write-ahead log is a mechanism used by databases to ensure data consistency and recoverability in case of a system failure. It's a journal that records all changes made to the database before they are written to the actual data files. This means that as soon as a transaction begins, its changes are first written to the log, and only then are those changes applied to the database.

## Step 2: How the Log Works During a Transaction
When a transaction starts, the database records the initial state of the transaction, including what data will be modified, in the log. This is the "write-ahead" part: the database writes a record of the planned changes before it actually makes them. As the transaction proceeds and data is modified, each change is also recorded in the log. If the transaction is committed (i.e., it's completed successfully), the database records this fact in the log as well, indicating that the transaction should be reflected in the main database files.
